summaries.example: Imagine that one class tries to explain why a toy car rolls down a ramp. A new explanation predicts the car’s path better, answers more questions, and helps the class test new ideas. That may count as progress. But simply doing more experiments, writing more pages, or becoming famous does not automatically mean the class learned more.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of scientific progress asks what it means for science to get better and how we can recognize that improvement. The answer depends on the part of science we are discussing. More funding, better instruments, or more skilled researchers may support science, but cognitive progress concerns advances in knowledge. Progress is not just development or change: it means improvement relative to a goal. Philosophers disagree about the best goal. Some emphasize solving important problems, making accurate predictions, giving unified explanations, gaining information, increasing understanding, or moving closer to truth. Measures such as publications and citations can help us judge progress, but they are only indicators. A theory may be replaced rather than simply added to, and older ideas may lose some successes. Therefore, scientific progress is not always a smooth pile of facts. It is a complex, fallible process in which people compare theories and revise their judgments.
key_ideas: Science can improve in several ways, such as better tools, better training, and better methods. But the entry mainly focuses on progress in knowledge.
Progress is different from mere change. To call something progress, we must say what goal or standard makes it better.
Counting papers, citations, or solved problems can give clues, but these numbers do not by themselves prove that knowledge has improved.
Some philosophers think progress means solving more important problems. Others connect it with truth, information, explanation, understanding, or reliable methods.
A new theory may replace an old one instead of simply adding facts to it. Even so, the new theory may preserve some successes of the old one.
Scientists can make mistakes, so claims about progress are judgments based on evidence rather than guarantees.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding scientific progress helps us judge claims about science carefully. It reminds us that a large number of experiments or papers is not the same as better knowledge. It also helps explain why scientists sometimes replace successful older ideas while still learning from them. Thinking about goals, evidence, and indicators can make us more thoughtful readers of scientific news and discoveries.

important_terms.definition: A change that is an improvement according to some goal or standard.
A neutral word for something becoming different or developing. Change is not always an improvement.
The growth or improvement of what science knows and understands.
A sign that helps us judge whether progress may have happened, even though the sign can sometimes mislead us.
The ability of an idea or theory to answer questions or solve scientific problems.
The idea that a scientific explanation can become closer to the truth, even if it is not completely true.

questions_to_think_about: If a scientist invents a faster instrument but learns nothing new, has science made cognitive progress?
Can an idea be useful for solving problems even if it is not completely true?
Why might counting the number of scientific papers give an incomplete picture of progress?
Should a new theory have to keep every success of an older theory?
What evidence would make you think that a scientific explanation is getting closer to the truth?

summaries.example: Suppose a new physical theory reproduces the successful predictions of an older theory in familiar cases, explains additional observations, and works in situations where the older theory fails. A realist might describe this as progress toward a more truthlike account of nature. A problem-solving philosopher might emphasize the new theory’s greater capacity to resolve anomalies. An instrumentalist might focus on its improved empirical success without claiming that its unobservable entities are real. The same historical change can therefore be assessed by different accounts of progress.
summaries.summary:
The entry examines a philosophical problem that is often hidden by the familiar claim that science progresses: what exactly is progress, and how can it be recognized? Progress is normative rather than merely descriptive. It means improvement relative to goals or standards, whereas development simply records change. Science contains several dimensions, but the central issue is cognitive progress—the advancement of knowledge-seeking or truth-seeking inquiry. Economic resources, professional status, education, instruments, and methods may promote cognitive progress without constituting it. Likewise, technological or social benefits may result from science without being identical to advances in scientific knowledge.

Theories of progress differ because they assign different weights to epistemic goals. Instrumentalists may emphasize empirical success, prediction, and problem-solving; realists may add truth or truthlikeness, the idea that successive theories can approach truth without accumulating only fully true statements. Other views stress explanatory and unifying power, simplicity, information, knowledge, or understanding. None of these measures is obviously sufficient alone. A theory can be informative but false, influential but misleading, or successful at solving problems while losing some problems addressed by its predecessor. Progress can therefore branch, involve theory replacement, and include losses as well as gains.

The entry also separates real progress from estimates of progress. Real progress is an objective improvement according to a chosen account, while estimated progress is a fallible judgment based on available evidence and probabilities. key_ideas: The concept of progress is normative and goal-relative. Calling a change progressive requires standards for what counts as improvement.

Science has economic, professional, educational, methodological, and cognitive dimensions. The entry concentrates on cognitive progress while distinguishing it from factors that promote or result from it.
Quality concerns how competently research is conducted, whereas progress concerns what the research achieves. High quality makes progress more likely but does not guarantee it.
Scientific indicators, including publication counts and citation measures, reveal activity or influence but cannot determine the semantic contribution of a work without expert assessment.
Major accounts of progress appeal to empirical success, problem-solving, explanation, unification, simplicity, information, truth, truthlikeness, knowledge, or understanding. These aims can conflict.

A distinction between real progress and estimated progress is important. A development may really improve a theory even if scientists cannot yet recognize that fact, while evidence-based estimates can be mistaken.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate matters because evaluations of science guide trust, research priorities, and judgments about past and present theories. It prevents simplistic equations such as more publications equals more progress or usefulness equals truth. It also clarifies why disagreement about science may concern not only evidence but the aims used to evaluate evidence: solving problems, explaining phenomena, predicting successfully, understanding mechanisms, or approaching truth. Examining these aims makes assessments of scientific achievement more explicit and less misleading.

important_terms.definition: A normative concept: a later stage is progressive when it is better than an earlier stage relative to specified standards or goals.
A descriptive term for change or development that does not, by itself, say that the result is better.
Progress understood as an advance in scientific knowledge, rather than in funding, status, training, or instruments.
The view that theories are tools for organizing observations and making predictions, without needing to be true descriptions of unobservable reality.
The view that scientific theories attempt to describe reality, including aspects that cannot be directly observed.
A theory’s success in resolving empirical and conceptual questions, including anomalies that rival theories may handle better.
A property of a theory that combines being informative with being close to the truth; it is often used to describe progress through successive imperfect theories.
A feature used to estimate progress, such as predictive success, citations, or solved problems; an indicator is not automatically a definition of progress.

questions_to_think_about: Can a theory count as progressive if it solves many problems but is entirely false, or does problem-solving require some connection with truth?
Should progress be measured by movement away from earlier ignorance, movement toward an unknown truth, or a combination of both?
Why do publication counts and citation indexes fail to define scientific progress?
Does replacing a theory undermine the idea that science is cumulative, or can progress preserve successes without preserving whole theories?
How should differences in historical standards of rationality affect our evaluation of scientists in the past?

summaries.example: A school science team studies local pond water. Team B uses a better test, notices that an earlier explanation does not fit some results, and proposes an explanation that predicts new results. It may have made progress even if it later needs correction. The team’s number of reports or popularity might show activity or impact, but those facts alone do not show that its explanation improved.
summaries.summary:
The philosophy of scientific progress studies how science changes and whether some changes count as improvements. It separates two questions: what progress is, and how we can recognize it. Progress is normative, meaning that it uses standards about what is better. Development and change are more neutral descriptions. The entry focuses especially on cognitive progress: advances in scientific knowledge and knowledge-seeking, rather than increases in funding, professional status, training, or equipment. Those other advances may support science, and science may produce technological or social benefits, but they are not automatically cognitive progress.

Philosophers offer competing accounts of the standards. One approach emphasizes empirical success and problem-solving: a later theory is better when it solves more important problems or handles more anomalies. Other approaches stress prediction, explanation, unification, simplicity, information, knowledge, understanding, or closeness to truth. Realists treat theories as attempts to describe reality, while instrumentalists treat them mainly as tools for organizing observations and predicting results. A theory can be useful without being regarded as a literally true description.

The entry warns against treating simple measurements as definitions. A publication count measures output, and citations can measure influence, but neither tells us exactly how much a work advances knowledge. Quality and progress are related but distinct: careful work raises the chance of success, yet even excellent research can fail, while luck can sometimes produce a valuable result. Finally, judgments of progress are fallible. Scientists may estimate progress from evidence, but later information can show that an earlier judgment was mistaken. Theor‌
key_ideas: The entry asks both what scientific progress means and how people can recognize it.
Progress is not the same as change. It requires a judgment that one stage is better according to some goal.
Science can improve through money, training, instruments, and methods, but the main focus is cognitive progress: better knowledge or inquiry.
A theory can gain support by solving problems, making predictions, explaining more, unifying different findings, or becoming simpler. Philosophers disagree about which achievements matter most.
Science may not grow like a perfectly neat pile of facts. New theories can reject, replace, reinterpret, or preserve parts of older theories.
Research indicators can be useful, but influence, quality, and progress are different. Experts must examine what a scientific work actually says and accomplishes.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us evaluate scientific claims without using overly simple scorecards. It shows why a famous, frequently cited, or technically impressive study may not make a major contribution to knowledge. It also explains why disagreements about science can persist even when people agree about the evidence: they may value different goals, such as prediction, explanation, practical usefulness, understanding, or truth. Learning these distinctions supports more careful thinking about scientific change.

important_terms.definition: An improvement from one stage to another when judged by a stated standard or goal.
A description of change over time that does not say whether the change is better or worse.
An advance in scientific knowledge or in the success of knowledge-seeking inquiry.
A way of organizing ideas or claims that helps explain observations and make predictions.
The ability of a theory to solve important empirical or conceptual problems and handle difficulties faced by rivals.
A measure or clue used to judge progress, such as predictive success, citations, or solved problems.
The view that theories aim to describe reality, including unobservable parts of it.
The idea that a theory can become more similar to the truth without simply adding fully certain truths.

questions_to_think_about: Why is calling a scientific change “progress” different from merely describing what happened?
Could a highly skilled research project fail to produce progress? Why?
What might be lost when a new theory replaces an old one?
Would you trust a theory more because it makes bold predictions, or because it is highly likely given current evidence?
How can a useful indicator of progress also be misleading?
